▸ On artificial intelligence • Buttondown

💡 Citing ethical, environmental, and financial harms fueled by venture capital, the author advocates a total boycott of generative AI.

This article distinguishes resource-intensive generative AI and LLMs from legacy, purpose-built machine learning models, criticizing the former for massive environmental costs, high compute expenses, and uncompensated data sourcing. The author argues that venture capital pressure forces startups to adopt generative AI to inflate valuations and automate labor, primarily serving to prevent capitalization table dilution for investors. Consequently, tech leaders sustain an artificially inflated financial bubble by intentionally overlooking the ethical, social, and practical harms of these technologies. Finding that the limited utility of generative tools fails to offset their systemic risks, the author advocates for a complete personal boycott of generative AI across software development, writing, and search.

📝 关键要点 (6 sections)
  • Defining Generative AI Scope: The author distinguishes energy-intensive generative AI and LLMs from older, purpose-built models like speech recognition. Generative models represent the core focus of the author's ethical and practical concerns.
  • Compute and Resource Waste: General-purpose LLMs incur massive compute, financial, and environmental costs during both training and inference. Using these models consumes unsustainable amounts of electricity and water while relying on stolen training content.
  • Investor Hype Over Utility: Venture capitalists push startups to adopt generative AI solely to chase inflated valuations rather than solve real business problems. Funding is increasingly tied to AI hype rather than product necessity or sustainable profitability.
  • Capitalization Tables and Labor: Generative AI is leveraged to replace human employees with automated agents, preventing capitalization table dilution for founders and VCs. This structural shift concentrates payouts among investors while cutting workers out of equity.
  • Financial Market Speculation: Tech investors treat AI as a high-stakes financial gamble to prevent a massive market correction. Corporate leaders overlook AI-driven harms and ethical risks because their financial survival depends on maintaining the hype.
  • Personal Ethical Stance: Finding no clear boundary for ethical usage, the author chooses to completely avoid generative AI for coding, writing, and search. The technology fails to provide enough value to justify compromising personal moral standards.

▸ Five software engineering roles for working with AI

💡 Software engineers operate across five AI collaboration roles, balancing increased delegation productivity against trade-offs like lost system context.

As human-AI software engineering interactions mature, developers operate across a spectrum of five distinct roles based on their desired level of technical oversight and delegation. Hands-on approaches include acting as a real-time pair programmer to build trust, an asynchronous delegator who leverages automated CI/CD safeguards to review agent PRs, or a system architect focusing on high-level design and component contracts. At higher levels of abstraction, engineers function as pipeline orchestrators automating agent workflows or as pure product evaluators who bypass code inspection entirely. Ultimately, senior engineers must balance the massive productivity gains of greater AI delegation against critical trade-offs, such as review fatigue, troubleshooting friction, and diminished ground-level context during system failures.

📝 关键要点 (6 sections)
  • AI Collaboration Spectrum: Human-AI software engineering interactions have evolved into a broad spectrum modeled after traditional team roles. Developers choose varying levels of hands-on involvement based on trust, productivity goals, and technical oversight.
  • The Observer Role: Functioning like a pair programmer, the developer actively monitors AI code generation in real time. While this builds trust for cautious engineers, productivity remains capped by manual review capacity and fatigue.
  • The Tech Lead: Developers author technical specs and delegate implementation to AI agents asynchronously, reviewing pull requests at completion. Heavy investment in automated testing and linting multiplies productivity while mitigating review fatigue.
  • The Architect Role: This approach prioritizes high-level system design, component boundaries, and infrastructure contracts over implementation details. Spot-checking generated code remains necessary to retain ground-level context for debugging system failures.
  • Engineering Manager Role: Developers build automated software pipelines that transform high-level requirements into delegated tasks for AI agents. The role centers on refining process flow, though distance from code can complicate troubleshooting when automated cycles fail.
  • Product Manager Role: Engineers engage exclusively with user experience, feature validation, and end outcomes without inspecting technical implementation. While execution is fast, complete detachment leaves creators vulnerable when deep structural bugs arise.

📰 Martin Fowler (2 articles)

▸ Fragments: September 8

💡 Cheap AI generation increases verification costs, system complexity, and legal friction, requiring stricter constraints and human oversight.

Although AI drastically reduces output generation costs, it does not lower verification costs, creating risks of technical debt, audience alienation, and software systems that become too complex for humans or models to maintain. To mitigate these issues, developers and organizations must prioritize rigorous verification over pure speed and enforce strict constraints on system size. Additionally, while integrating autonomous AI agents accelerates development output, it challenges human oversight and creates growing tension around maintaining a full understanding of the codebase. Finally, the broader industry faces legal friction over unconsented copyrighted training data alongside the ongoing threat of losing foundational digital history.

📝 关键要点 (6 sections)
  • Generation Versus Verification: AI drastically reduces the cost of generating output but not the cost of verifying it. This imbalance risks creating 'counterfeit utility' and technical debt unless organizations incentivize rigorous verification over pure speed.
  • Inauthenticity of LLM Writing: Readers quickly spot LLM-generated text and overwhelmingly reject it in favor of an authentic human voice. Authors who rely heavily on AI generation risk alienating their audience and damaging their reputation.
  • Copyright and Consent Dynamics: Major music publishers are suing AI developers over the unauthorized use of copyrighted works in training datasets. Regulators must account for this unconsented foundation even if the societal utility of LLMs is high.
  • AI System Complexity Runaway: AI models will eventually generate software systems too complex for humans or the models themselves to maintain. Developers must maintain strict constraints on system size to prevent uncontrollable complexity.
  • Preserving Legacy UX Wisdom: The disappearance of Kathy Sierra’s seminal blog 'Creating Passionate Users' highlights the fragility of digital history. Preserving foundational insights from web blogging remains essential for modern practitioners.
  • Symmathesy and Agentic Coding: Incorporating autonomous AI agents into development teams accelerates output but challenges human oversight. Developers face growing tension between leveraging agent speed and maintaining full understanding of their codebase.

▸ Do you even need a presentation?

💡 Reserve slide decks for live storytelling, relying on written documents, infodecks, or interactive tools for asynchronous communication.

Slide decks should be reserved primarily for high-impact, live storytelling, whereas linear written documents provide superior context and editing efficiency for asynchronous corporate communication. Text-based artifacts simplify reorganization, streamline async collaboration, and produce structured data that is easily parsed by AI tools. For lighter visual communication, "infodecks" effectively merge concise text with visual metaphors, though they require significant information design effort. Additionally, leveraging web technologies to build lightweight interactive applications dynamically manages reader cognitive load far better than static text or spreadsheets.

📝 关键要点 (5 sections)
  • Defining True Presentations: A presentation is an act of storytelling and interaction rather than just a slideshow. Slide decks should be reserved for high-impact scenarios where narrative, timing, and emotion create additional meaning.
  • Prioritizing Linear Documents: Most corporate information sharing is best handled by standard written documents rather than fragmented slide decks. Linear writing helps readers systematically build understanding without losing critical context in asynchronous settings.
  • Document Tooling Advantages: Writing tools streamline editing, simplify language, and enable seamless async collaboration. Reorganizing text in a document is faster than tweaking slides and creates low-context artifacts that are easier for AI to summarize.
  • Leveraging Visual Infodecks: Infodecks use slide creation tools as an accessible layout solution to combine concise text with visual metaphors for light reading. Creating effective infodecks requires clear writing and significant information design effort.
  • Interactive Web Artifacts: Modern web harnesses enable non-developers to build simple interactive applications using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. These interactive tools dynamic manage reader cognitive load better than static text or spreadsheets.

▸ ActivityPub - Is it worth defending against replay attacks and message/signature time skew?

💡 Strict timestamp validation in ActivityPub harms interoperability for minor security gains, making message idempotency the superior defense.

ActivityPub message payload timestamps are inherently unreliable for validating request freshness due to network latency, retry loops, and implementation quirks, requiring applications to evaluate transport-layer HTTP signature parameters (`Date` or `created`) instead. Currently, the federated ecosystem lacks a strict standard for acceptable clock skew, resulting in disparate implementation tolerances ranging from strict 30-second windows to hour-long allowances or complete non-enforcement. While signature timestamp validation primarily defends against HTTP request replay attacks, accepting delayed payloads poses minimal practical security risk for standard ActivityPub operations. Ultimately, strict signature window enforcement offers marginal security gains at the expense of federation interoperability, making content integrity and message idempotency the primary lines of defense.
